pages.text: Mamle used to swim in the river when she was small. The water was clear enough to see her toes. Today, on the way to school, she stopped on the bridge and stared. The river was thick and brown, like cocoa drink. “Mr Appiah,” she said in class, “what happened to our river?”
sentences: Mamle used to swim in the river when she was small.
The water was clear enough to see her toes.
Today, on the way to school, she stopped on the bridge and stared.
The river was thick and brown, like cocoa drink.
“Mr Appiah,” she said in class, “what happened to our river?”
pages.alt: A girl stands on a bridge looking down at a thick brown river; a faded picture shows the same river clear.

pages.text: Mr Appiah brought two jars. One held clean water. In the other he stirred a spoon of soil. “This is how cloudy water looks,” he said. “Scientists measure it with a word: turbidity. The more tiny bits of soil and clay in the water, the higher the turbidity.” Ntow held the jars up to the window and tried to see through each one.
sentences: Mr Appiah brought two jars.
One held clean water.

“This is how cloudy water looks,” he said.
“Scientists measure it with a word: turbidity.
The more tiny bits of soil and clay in the water, the higher the turbidity.” Ntow held the jars up to the window and tried to see through each one.
pages.alt: A teacher holds two jars to the light, one clear and one muddy, while children look through them.

pages.text: “Why is our river so muddy?” asked Ntow. “One big reason is illegal mining, which people call galamsey,” said Mr Appiah. “Diggers dig in or beside the river and wash soil and gravel in the water. The mud runs downstream. Farming, timber cutting and sand winning can also add soil. But galamsey is named again and again for rivers like the Pra, the Ankobra, the Birim and the Offin.”

The mud runs downstream.
Farming, timber cutting and sand winning can also add soil.
But galamsey is named again and again for rivers like the Pra, the Ankobra, the Birim and the Offin.”
pages.alt: Diggers wash soil beside a river while brown water spreads downstream, drawn without showing any faces.

pages.text: “How muddy is it?” asked Mamle. “Scientists use a unit called NTU,” said Mr Appiah. “A minister said that the normal range is 0 to 500, and that some rivers have been measured at 5,000 to 12,000. Another writer says above 10,000. Numbers differ between reports and places, but all agree that it is far too high.”

Another writer says above 10,000.
Numbers differ between reports and places, but all agree that it is far too high.”
pages.alt: A measuring scale showing 0 to 500 in green and a tall brown bar far above it.

pages.text: “What does it do to our water supply?” asked Ntow. “Our water plant takes water from the river and cleans it,” said Mr Appiah. “When the river is very muddy, the filters clog, the plant needs more chemicals and the cost goes up. The Ghana Water Company has had to shut plants, such as at Daboase and Kyebi, when the water was too muddy to treat. Then taps run dry.”
sentences: “What does it do to our water supply?” asked Ntow.

“When the river is very muddy, the filters clog, the plant needs more chemicals and the cost goes up.
The Ghana Water Company has had to shut plants, such as at Daboase and Kyebi, when the water was too muddy to treat.
Then taps run dry.”
pages.alt: A water treatment plant with a clogged filter and a tap that gives only a drip.

pages.text: “And the fish?” asked Mamle. “Mud clouds the water so that plants cannot get sunlight and fish struggle to breathe and to find food,” said Mr Appiah. “Some miners also use chemicals like mercury, which we will study next term. A scientist says more than sixty per cent of Ghana’s water bodies are polluted by illegal mining. That is a claim we should check, but it shows the size of the problem.”

A scientist says more than sixty per cent of Ghana’s water bodies are polluted by illegal mining.
That is a claim we should check, but it shows the size of the problem.”
pages.alt: A river with few fish and muddy banks, next to a picture of a clear river full of fish.

pages.text: Mr Appiah let the children make a filter with sand, gravel, cloth and a cut bottle. They poured the muddy jar through it. The water came out clearer, but not clean. “A filter like this takes out some mud,” he said. “It cannot take out mercury or germs. That is why prevention is better than cure: keep the river from being muddied in the first place.”

pages.alt: Children pour muddy water through a homemade bottle filter into a jar while others watch.

pages.text: The children wrote on a poster: A healthy river needs healthy banks. Ntow drew trees along the water. Mamle drew a clear river with children swimming. “Scientists think it could take ten to twenty years of steady work to heal our rivers,” said Mr Appiah. “That is longer than you have been alive. So you can be the grown-ups who finish it.” The end.
